claims.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi', which covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud was nearly impossible with AWS CDK.
In its early days, SST was built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK), which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.

AWS CDK and CloudFormation act as a code generator, producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is executed to deploy resources, so the code the developer writes is not the code that runs during deployment.
AWS CDK is AWS-only, while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployments are slower than Pulumi's because of CloudFormation; Pulumi offers faster direct execution.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, while AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
AWS CDK state management uses a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment instead of generating an intermediary format.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Insights provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities.
Pulumi has built-in extensibility features including custom providers and dynamic components.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to customize deployments.
Pulumi allows defining infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploying across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments enables advanced deployment workflows, documented at /docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' at /resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications, where components are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation; once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine and also bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
Nitric and Defang also run application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building their own diff, state, and provider layer.
The SST team has said, repeatedly since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define app infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs 'What is SST' page says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi` plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds, and others (`@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`), alongside the Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumiverse/vercel`).
The SST repository is at `anomalyco/sst` (formerly `sst/sst`) on GitHub, with the file at platform/package.json on the dev branch.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) translates each resource into cloud API calls via Terraform-bridged providers.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers with the Pulumi engine.
The Pulumi engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding Pulumi programs inside other tools, and the same provider bridge lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.

Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider (DefangLabs/pulumi-defang) is described as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`".
Nitric, Defang, and SST expose a narrower, more opinionated interface to their users while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger following on GitHub (more stars) than SST itself.
SST's dependency on the Pulumi engine has not changed as a result of the team's work on opencode, and SST releases and download numbers show it is not being abandoned.
The team's attention to opencode has not changed SST's release cadence.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state; its components use Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides guardrails enforced centrally by a platform team, and components share infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components do not require leaving the Pulumi engine SST already uses.
SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
SST isn't the only project to build on the Pulumi engine; other tools make the same choice.
SST is a strong fit for teams wanting an opinionated, full-stack application framework with infrastructure and code defined together.
Embedding the Pulumi engine gives a framework a production-grade provisioning engine and hundreds of cloud providers.
The linked post 'AWS CDK vs Pulumi: Why SST Chose Pulumi' exists at /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/ and tells the story of SST's move off CDK.
